author: Ethan's photos and checks of the variegated Monstera cutting (November 11, 2026)

plants.aliases: Variegated Monstera cutting; Swiss cheese plant (variegated); cutting from the mother plant
plants.location: East-facing window sill, in a tall clear container of filtered water
plants.container: Tall clear plastic jar of filtered water, with the root nub and cut end underwater, leaves in the air
plants.id_basis: Ethan: a cutting from a larger mother plant. Large heart-shaped, unsplit leaves, green with irregular cream splashes and fine cream speckles all over, which is how 'Thai Constellation' looks and matches the two pages P-094 and P-095. A plain albo has big clean white sectors and no speckling, so it fits less well. There is no tag on the cutting, and which plant it came from is not recorded.
plants.id_alternatives:
Monstera deliciosa 'Thai Constellation'
Monstera deliciosa 'Albo Variegata' (less likely: no speckling)
Monstera deliciosa 'Aurea' (cream-yellow, not speckled)
plants.id_improve:
Which plant the cutting came from (P-094, P-095 or another), and its tag or source
The first new leaf once it roots: 'Thai Constellation' keeps the speckles and splashes
plants.temp_notes: Tropical: keep it above 55 F. Chilling marks the cream parts first.
plants.humidity_notes: The cream patches brown at the edges in dry air; 55-65% is a good target under the light.
plants.light_summary: Bright indirect light; the east window is gentle enough, but no hot direct sun on the cream parts
plants.light_hours: 6-8 h bright indirect, or a grow light 12 h
plants.light_notes: The tag's 'full sun' is nursery shade-house advice. Indoors, direct midday sun scorches the cream areas (the browning on the palest leaf). Too little light gives small, slow leaves.
plants.winter_summary: A tropical aroid: indoors all year in Round Rock, under the grow light in winter.
plants.winter_triggers: Already indoors; keep it above 60 F and away from cold glass.
plants.winter_steps:
Grow light 12 h a day.
Let the sphagnum dry on top before watering; water less from November to February.
No feeding in winter.
Keep the moss pole damp so the aerial roots take hold.
plants.indoor_setup: Under the grow light 12-18 in away for 12 h, or a bright east or north-east window. Humidity 50% or more. Tie new growth to the pole as it climbs: leaves get bigger and split sooner.
plants.health_summary: A rootless cutting with two leaves and one root nub. One leaf has browned, dried and collapsed; the other holds up better but has brown patches. The node, the nub and the cut end were all checked on November 11 and are firm, green and odourless, with no slime, so the cutting itself is alive. A cutting with no roots cannot replace the water its leaves lose, so sag and leaf loss are common; the exact cause here is not confirmed.
plants.health_observations:
Two leaves on long stalks; one browned, dry and collapsed
The other leaf has brown patches and a limp tip
Node where the leaf meets the stem: green, firm, no smell
One root nub, firm, no film, no smell
Cut end: dry brown callus, firm, no film, no smell
Water 3 days old and clear
Only the lower stem is under water; the leaves stay dry
plants.health_steps:
Change the water every 3 to 5 days and keep only the root nub and cut end under water.
Bright indirect light; keep it out of hot direct sun, which scorches the cream parts.
Keep it warm: rooting slows a lot below about 70°F.
Cut off the collapsed leaf once it is fully dead, so it cannot rot in the water or touch the other leaf.
Be patient: variegated cuttings often take 4 to 8 weeks or more to root.
If the node ever turns soft, dark or smelly, trim back to firm tissue and change the water.
When roots are about an inch long, move it into perlite, sphagnum or a gritty mix; water roots are fragile in soil.
plants.notes: A cutting from a larger mother plant, in water since before November 11, 2026 (the exact day it was cut is not recorded). Photographed and checked on November 11: node, nub and cut end firm and odourless. Ethan can tell the app which plant it came from and when it was cut.
plants.water_notes: Water when the top inch of sphagnum is dry and the pot is light, soaking through and draining the saucer. Roughly weekly in summer under the light, every 10-14 days in winter. Sphagnum holds a lot of water: the main risk is keeping it wet. Yellow leaves with soft stems mean too wet.
plants.soil_medium: Chunky aroid mix: bark, perlite or pumice, a little coco coir or sphagnum. The current sphagnum and lava rock works if it is allowed to dry between waterings.
plants.nutrients: Regular light feeding; the plant grows slowly and burns with strong feed.
plants.pests_watch:
Thrips: silvery streaks and black specks, deformed new leaves (common on variegated Monstera)
Spider mites: stippling and webbing in dry air
Scale and mealybugs at the leaf stalk bases
plants.pest_steps:
Check both sides of each leaf and the stalk bases every two weeks, with a torch.
Wipe leaves; treat thrips with spinosad or insecticidal soap and repeat weekly for a month.
Quarantine new plants.
plants.growth_habit: A climbing aroid: heart-shaped juvenile leaves now, splits and holes (fenestrations) once it climbs; the cream variegation is stable (tissue-culture)
plants.native_range: The species is from southern Mexico to Panama (rain forest climber); this cultivar came from a Thai tissue-culture lab.
plants.conservation_status: Not applicable: a cultivar; the species is widespread.
plants.invasive: Not a risk here (invasive in some tropical islands).
plants.bloom: Rare indoors (a creamy spathe on a mature plant).
plants.fruit: The edible "fruit salad" fruit of the species, on mature outdoor plants only; unripe fruit burns the mouth.
plants.danger_humans: Leaves and stems contain calcium oxalate crystals: chewing burns the mouth and throat.
plants.danger_animals: Toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA): drooling, mouth pain, vomiting.
plants.propagation: A stem cutting with a node and an aerial root, rooted in water, sphagnum or perlite. Choose a node whose leaf has both green and cream.
